comment: Ranking ivosidenib first because it reads like placebo on safety buys the cleanest toxicity bill in the dossier and the smallest payoff: ORR 2% (3/124) and an ITT OS that missed at HR 0.69, p=0.060 (pmid:32416072). If the panel hands us an FGFR2 fusion (ORR 42%) or an NTRK fusion (ORR 79%), leading with the 2% shrinkage option spends the patient's one shot at depth of response on disease stabilization. I would let effect size, not the lowest grade-3 rate, set rank-1 once the test reads positive.

I picked your rank-5 rather than your rank-1 because burying T-DXd as a cautionary flag throws out the largest HER2 signal here: in the central IHC 3+ slice the ORR is 61.3% with mDoR 22.1 months (pmid:37870536), against zanidatamab's 41.3% (pmid:37423227). You are right that the registered biliary-cohort number is 22% and the ILD at 10.5% with three deaths is real, so this stays gated on a confirmed IHC 3+ read with explicit pulmonary monitoring. But on a true 3+ tumor that response magnitude is the upside I would chase, not flag.

Every option on your list is NCCN category 2A, so the guideline tier does not actually separate them, and you used it to seat the ORR 2% option (pmid:32416072) above futibatinib at ORR 42% and the fusion agents. When the consensus grade is flat across the whole panel, the tiebreaker that matters in advanced disease is depth of response on a positive test, not which 2A was listed first. I would re-rank toward the bigger signal the moment a feature confirms.

A 0.5 efficacy/toxicity weight with empty toxicity_vetoes does not mean pick the gentlest drug; it means do not throw away response to dodge a side effect the patient never vetoed. Larotrectinib at ORR 79% with grade 3 in only 13% (pmid:32092306) honors a balanced weight at least as well as ivosidenib's placebo-like profile and ORR 2%, and it carries far more upside. Read plainly, the balanced setting tells me to weight the high-response oral agents up, not down.

On safety we agree: larotrectinib is the gentlest thing on the board, grade 3 in 13% and grade 4 under 1% with no treatment-related deaths across 260 patients (pmid:32092306), and I gave it a top-three slot myself for exactly that. Where I split from you is seating it at rank 1 on a sub-1% NTRK prevalence, which spends the lead slot on the read least likely to come back positive. A clean toxicity profile earns my trust on what to give once a fusion confirms; it does not earn rank 1 ahead of the 15-20% IDH1 and 10-15% FGFR2 axes the same panel resolves.

You listed T-DXd at rank 5 to flag rather than endorse, and I am hardening that flag into a formal veto: adjudicated drug-related ILD ran 10.5% with three treatment-related deaths (pmid:37870536), and intake supplied no pulmonary baseline, no organ-function labs, and no DLCO to gate against. This is the uncharacterized severe long-tail my prior refuses without dedicated mitigation, and zanidatamab covers the HER2 lane at a 3% grade-3 ejection-fraction signal with a standard echo algorithm (pmid:37423227). Veto contingent on a documented HER2 IHC 3+ read plus a baseline pulmonary assessment and a written ILD-monitoring plan; absent those, it does not enter the recommendation.

Seating futibatinib above pemigatinib on an ESMO-MCBS score of 3 versus 2 leans on a benefit metric that does not price the toxicity gap inside the FGFR2 lane. Grade 3 hyperphosphatemia reached 30% on futibatinib (pmid:36652354) against essentially none on pemigatinib, where the on-target effect was 55% any-grade with no grade 3-4 events (pmid:32203698). At a comparable ORR I take the lower-grade burden and the longer post-approval record, so I reverse your within-lane order; the MCBS point does not outweigh a 30-point grade-3 difference.

I will not penalize the IV route either, and pembrolizumab's immune-mediated toxicity is genuinely well-characterized with an established management algorithm, grade 3-5 TRAEs at 14.6% (pmid:31682550). My reservation is what the basket does not give: KEYNOTE-158 reports no CCA-specific subgroup ORR, so the biliary magnitude is inferred from a 27-tumor pool admitted on the biomarker. I would hold it as a contingency on a confirmed MSI-H/dMMR or TMB-high read, with the caveat that no organ-function baseline was supplied to confirm immune-AE monitoring is feasible.

The 79% ORR you lead with is a pooled phase 1/2 basket across many tumor types with no biliary cohort reported (pmid:32092306), so what you are quoting is cross-tumor extrapolation standing in for CCA-specific data we do not have. Single-arm, surrogate endpoint, open-label ascertainment, and a sub-1% prevalence to boot; that is the thinnest indication base on the board to seat at rank 1. Ranking expected effect ahead of evidence quality is your prior, not mine, and I would not put the least CCA-anchored row first.

We land on the same rank-1 and the same reason: ClarIDHy is the one RoB2-Low randomized phase 3 here, met its registered PFS endpoint (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.25-0.54), and reads near placebo on grade 3+ (pmid:32416072). My one correction to your framing is the survival claim: the registered ITT OS missed at HR 0.69, p=0.060, and the 0.46 figure is an RPSFT crossover adjustment after 70% crossed over, so it is a sensitivity analysis, not a clean result. Buying disease control is the honest pitch; an OS benefit is not.

You seated futibatinib above pemigatinib on an ESMO-MCBS score of 3 versus 2, but that metric is scored off two separate single-arm trials with no head-to-head, so it cannot adjudicate a within-lane order the way a randomized comparison would. Both rows are single-arm phase 2 on a surrogate ORR endpoint (pmid:36652354, pmid:32203698); the MCBS point and the underlying NCCN 2A both encode expert judgment over the same uncontrolled data, not a higher tier of evidence. I agree the FGFR2 lane belongs near the top because two independent trials converge on the axis, which is the nearest thing to replication in this dossier, but I would not let a cross-trial benefit score break the futibatinib-versus-pemigatinib tie.

Honoring prefers_trials and declining to penalize the IV route are both defensible, and I am not contesting either. The evidence problem is what neither KEYNOTE-158 row gives you: no CCA-specific subgroup ORR is published in the MSI-H analysis (pmid:31682550) or the TMB-high analysis (pmid:32919526), so the biliary magnitude is inferred from a 27-tumor pool the patient enters on the biomarker alone. That is a real gap to name when surfacing this option, not a reason to drop it, since a confirmed MSI-H or TMB-high read still admits the patient to the labeled indication.

NCCN BTC v2.2025 does list larotrectinib, via the tumor-agnostic NTRK route, so the drug itself is on consensus. My problem is the rank. Seating a sub-1% NTRK read first, above the IDH1 axis at 15-20% and FGFR2 at 10-15% that the same guidelines flag as the high-yield biomarkers to test for in this disease, inverts the testing priority the consensus actually sets (pmid:32092306). Effect size if the test happens to read positive is not how the panel orders a biomarker workup.

We agree both FGFR2 agents are NCCN BTC v2.2025 category 2A, so the consensus tier does not split them. You reversed my within-lane order on a 30-point grade-3 hyperphosphatemia gap (pmid:36652354 vs pmid:32203698), which is a fair toxicity read. But ESMO-MCBS v1.1 scores futibatinib at 3 against pemigatinib at 2, and that benefit metric already weighs magnitude against the safety profile, so the European consensus lands futibatinib ahead even after pricing the toxicity you are citing.

You are right there is no head-to-head, so the ESMO-MCBS v1.1 score of 3 versus 2 is built from two separate single-arm trials (pmid:36652354, pmid:32203698). Where I push back: that score and the NCCN BTC v2.2025 category 2A are the collective expert calibration of exactly the uncontrolled data you are reading, not a separate evidence tier you can wave off. When a randomized comparison does not exist, that calibration is what breaks the within-lane tie; flattening the order discards the one structured judgment the field has actually made over these two trials.

Surfacing TYRA-200 (nct:NCT06160752) under prefers_trials is reasonable as a resistance-directed option, and I have no quarrel with naming it. The quarrel is where it sits: no society lists tyra-200 in BTC, so it is pre-guideline, and folding it into a ranked therapeutic pick next to the NCCN BTC v2.2025 category 2A futibatinib blurs the line. Trial enrollment is the guideline-aligned route for an off-guideline agent; the ranked recommendation is not.

On the patient's preferences I am with you more than against you: larotrectinib is oral, the grade 3 rate is 13%, and there is an open basket trial (NCT02576431) that satisfies prefers_trials cleanly (pmid:32092306). Where I pull back is the rank. The only ranking signal the patient actually gave is prefers_trials, and the balanced 0.5 weight says nothing about chasing the rarest read first. From where the patient sits, seating a sub-1% NTRK result at rank 1 means the lead recommendation is the one they are least likely to ever get to act on. I would order the trial menu so the axes a positive test can realistically return for this patient come first.

Ivosidenib genuinely fits the file: oral, placebo-like grade 3+, open registration trial for prefers_trials (pmid:32416072, NCT02989857). But your whole ranking logic leans on safety as the tiebreaker, and the patient set the efficacy/toxicity weight to 0.5, not toward tolerability. There are no toxicity_vetoes on file. Reading the preference plainly, a balanced weight does not license seating the ORR 2% option above futibatinib at 42% on the strength of a near-placebo profile. I would keep ivosidenib in the mix on its trial fit and its clean tolerability, without letting an unstated safety tilt set the order.

Your evidence-quality read is careful and I do not dispute the ClarIDHy facts: registered PFS met, ITT OS missed at p=0.060, the 0.46 is crossover modeling (pmid:32416072). My dissent is on whose ranking this is. The patient stated one preference, prefers_trials=true, and your list never engages it. Ranking strictly on RoB tier is your prior, not theirs. Every option you rank has an open trial route, so for this patient the order should at least register that preference somewhere rather than collapse entirely onto evidence grade. I would name the trial fit alongside the evidence call, not in place of it.

You dissented on my surfacing TYRA-200 (NCT06160752) because no society lists it in BTC. For a guideline-driven board that is fair, but it reads the preference file backwards. The patient set prefers_trials=true, which is the single explicit value on record. An off-guideline trial for a patient who has progressed on a first FGFR inhibitor is exactly the option that preference asks me to put in front of them, not the one to fence off because consensus has not caught up. I keep it labeled as a trial rather than a ranked therapeutic pick, but for a trial-preferring patient, pre-guideline status is a reason to surface it, not bury it.
